package_info.package_versions: Affected versions distributed after build environment compromise (exact versions not specified)
package_info.why_malicious: The 3CX Desktop Client was compromised via a software supply chain attack, where state-sponsored threat actors tampered with the build environment and injected a backdoor into the digitally signed application. This backdoor enabled remote command execution and data exfiltration, and was distributed to customers as a legitimate update.

execution_context.trigger: At application runtime, after user launches the 3CX Desktop Client
execution_context.file_location: Injected into the main application binary of the 3CX Desktop Client (Windows/macOS), typically in the executable file (e.g., 3CXDesktopApp.exe or 3CXDesktopApp.app/Contents/MacOS/3CXDesktopApp)
required_permissions: network (for outbound connections to C2 servers)
filesystem (for reading and potentially exfiltrating local data)
process (for executing arbitrary commands or scripts)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Backdoor code injected into the 3CX Desktop Client binary. The report describes this as a module that, once the application is running, establishes outbound connections to attacker-controlled command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, receives remote instructions, and can execute arbitrary commands or exfiltrate data. The exact code is not shown in the report.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At application runtime, the injected code establishes an outbound connection to a remote command-and-control server, receives attacker instructions, and executes arbitrary commands or exfiltrates files from the host system, resulting in unauthorized remote access and potential data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The injected code is not present in the official 3CX source code and enables covert remote access and command execution by unauthorized parties, which is not expected in legitimate desktop communication software.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate desktop client applications should not contain hidden modules that establish unauthorized network connections or allow remote command execution without user knowledge or consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote support or management tools may have similar capabilities, but only with explicit user consent, clear notification, and transparent operation. In this case, the functionality is hidden and unauthorized.
key_indicators: Presence of code in the application binary not found in official source repositories
Outbound network connections from the 3CX Desktop Client to suspicious or attacker-controlled domains
Ability to execute arbitrary system commands or scripts from within the client process
Unexpected changes in the digital signature or hash of the application binary
Persistence of the backdoor code across application updates

attack_chain.action: State-sponsored attackers compromise the 3CX build environment, gaining access to the software development pipeline.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is injected into the 3CX Desktop Client application binary during the build process.

attack_chain.action: Malicious backdoor code is added to the 3CX Desktop Client binary, embedding remote access and command execution capabilities.
attack_chain.leads_to: The compromised application is digitally signed and distributed to customers via official update channels.

attack_chain.action: Customers download and install the signed, but compromised, 3CX Desktop Client on their systems.
attack_chain.leads_to: The backdoor code is present and ready to execute on customer endpoints.

attack_chain.action: Upon execution, the backdoor establishes outbound connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure and enables remote access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attackers can remotely execute commands, exfiltrate data, and potentially move laterally within the victim's environment.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected outbound network connections initiated by 3CX Desktop Client processes to domains or IPs not associated with 3CX's legitimate infrastructure
Execution of code or modules within the 3CX Desktop Client binary that are not present in official source code or known-good builds
Presence of remote command execution or scripting capabilities in the 3CX Desktop Client, which is not a remote support tool
Persistence of unauthorized modules or code across application updates
file_indicators: Modified or anomalous 3CX Desktop Client binaries (e.g., 3CXDesktopApp.exe, 3CXDesktopApp.app/Contents/MacOS/3CXDesktopApp) with hashes differing from official releases
Unexpected changes in the digital signature or certificate chain of the application binary
Presence of additional or suspicious DLLs or modules loaded by the 3CX Desktop Client process
network_indicators: Connections from the 3CX Desktop Client to known command-and-control domains or IP addresses associated with the 3CX supply chain compromise (as listed in threat intelligence reports)
Unusual or encrypted traffic patterns from the 3CX Desktop Client to external destinations not documented in official 3CX network requirements
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor the integrity of 3CX Desktop Client binaries by comparing file hashes and digital signatures against official releases. Analyze network traffic from 3CX Desktop Client processes for connections to known C2 domains or IPs, and flag any unexpected outbound connections. Inspect running processes for unauthorized modules or evidence of remote command execution. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators to identify compromised installations and respond accordingly.
